d:chapter.d:title: Conic Sections
d:chapter.d:para: In this chapter we will study parabola, ellipse and hyperbola, their properties and elements like tangents and normals. The study of conic sections combines geometry and algebra. Using the coordinate plane, every conic can be represented by an equation in $x$ and $y$, allowing geometric properties to be studied analytically. Conics have rich mathematical structures involving focus, directrix, axis, eccentricity, tangents, normals, and chords.
Pair of straight lines, circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas are sections of a right circular cone by a plane, and so they are called conic sections.

As you can see in the that when a plane cuts the right circular cone perpendicular to the axis of the cone then we get a circle, when the plane cuts the cone parallel to the generator we get a parabola, when the plane is parallel to the axis we get hyperbola, and when the cone is neither parallel nor perpendicular to axis or generator we get an ellipse.

d:sect1.d:title: Definition
d:sect1.d:para: A conic section is defined as the locus of a point, which moves in a plane such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point and a fixed line is a constant.

The fixed point is called the focus and the fixed line the directrix of the conic section. The constant ratio is called eccentricity of the curve and is usually denoted by $e$. One such conic section is shown below:

If $e = 1$, then the resulting coninc is a parabola, if $e < 1$, then the resulting conic is an ellipse, and if $e > 1$, then the resulting conic is a hyperbola. In the given diagram $\frac{PS}{PN} = e$.
The straight line perpendicular from the focus to the directrix is called the axis of the conic. The point of intersection of the conic and its axis us called the vertex of the conic.
In the given diagram $S$ is the focus, $AN$ the directrix, $AS$ is the axis and $A$ is the vertex of the conic.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Conic
d:sect2.d:para: Let $S(\alpha, \beta)$ be the focus and $QN$ the directrix whose equation is $Ax + By + C = 0$.
Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the conic section. From $P$ draw $PN \perp QN$. Let $e$ be the eccentricity, then by definition $\frac{PS}{PN} = e \Rightarrow PS^2 = e^2PN^2$.
$PS^2 = (x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2$ and $PN^2 = \frac{(Ax + By + C)^2}{A^2 + B^2}$

$\Rightarrow (x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2 = \frac{e^2(A x + B y + C)^2}{A^2 + B^2}$, which on simplification will have the form $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$, where $a, b, c, f, g, h$ are constants.
Corollary: Let the focus $S$ lie on the directrix $QN$ and $S$ be taken as the origin and $QN$ be taken as the $y$-axis. Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the conic then
$\frac{PS}{PN} = e \Rightarrow \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}{|x|} = e \Rightarrow \left(e^2 - 1\right)x^2 = y^2$, which is a pair of straight lines through the focus or the origin.

Corollary: The general equation of the second degree $ax^2 + 2y^2 + 2hxy + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ represents a parabols if $h^2 = ab$ and $\Delta \neq 0$, where $\Delta = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2$ or alternatively a second degree equation represents a parabola if second degree terms form a complete square and $\Delta neq 0$.
The second degree equation will represent an ellipse if $h^2 < ab$. We will see that a circle is a special case of an ellipse.
The second degree equation will represent a hyperbola if $h^2 > ab$ and $\Delta \neq 0$ and a pair of straight lines if $\Delta = 0$.

d:sect1.d:title: Parabola
d:sect1.d:para: A parabola is the locus of a point which moves so that its distance from a fixed point, called the focus, is equal to the distance from a fixed line, called the directrix.
The straight line perpendicular from the focus to the directrix is called the axis of the parabola.
The equation of the parabola can be obtained if its directrix and focus are given.

Let $S$ be the focus and $QM$ the directrix of the parabola. From $S$ draw $SQ$ perpendicular to the directrix. Let $OP$ be the middle point of $QS$. Take $O$ as the origin and $OS$ as the $x$-axis and $OY$ through $O$ perpendicular to $OS$ as the $y$-axis.
Now $S = (a, 0)$ and the equation of $QM$ is $x = -a$. Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the parabola. Join $PS$ and drop perpendicular $PM$ on $QM$.
Be definition of the parabola $PS = PM \Rightarrow (x - a)^2 + y^2 = |x + a|^2$ \[y^2 = 4a x\label{eq:6.1}\tag{6.1}\]

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: If the point $(x, y)$ lies on the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ then point $(-x, -y)$ will also lie on the parabola. Hence, the parabola is symmatrical about its axis.
The point of intersection of the axis of a parabola and the parabola itself is called the vertex if the parabola.
If the perpendicular drawn from a point $P$ to the axis of the parabola meets the parabola at its symmateric point $P'$ then $PP'$ is called a double oridinate.

The double ordinate which passes through the focus is called the latus recturm of the parabola. The length of latus rectum of $y^2 = 4ax$ is $4a$.
The equation of the latus ractum of the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ is $x = a$.
Joining any two points on a parabola yields a line segment called chord.
If a chord passes through focus of a parabola is called focal chord.
The distance of any point on a parabola from the focus of the parabola is callled focal distance.

d:sect1.d:para: The other parabolas having the same length of latus rectum as that of $y^2 = 4ax$ are $y^2 + 4a x = 0, x^2 = 4ay$ and $x^2 + 4a y = 0$.

d:sect2.d:title: Intersection of a Line and a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Consider a straight line given by the equation $y = mx + c$ and a parabola given by the equation $y^2 = 4ax$.
Solving the equations gives us $(m x + c)^2 = 4a x \Rightarrow m^2x^2 + 2x(m c - 2a) + c^2 = 0$.

The above equation, which is a quadratic equation in $x$ will have two roots. If the roots are real i.e. $(mc - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 > 0$, then the will cut the parabola at two different points. If $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 = 0$, then there will be a repeated root and the line will be a tangent to the parabola and if $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 < 0$, then roots will be imaginary and the line will not inttersect with the parabola.
We see that $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 = 0$ is the condition for tangency. Thus, \[ c = \frac{a}{m} \tag{6.2}\]
Thus, any line of the form $y = mx + a/m$ will be a tangent to the parabola.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Tangent at a Given Point on a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of parabola be $y^2 = 4a x$. Let $P = (x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$ be any two points on the parabola. The equation of $PQ$ will be given by
Since both the points lie on the parabola, therefore $y_1^2 = 4a x_1$ and $y_2^2 = 4a x_2$
Subtracting these two equations yields $(y_2 + y_1)(y_2 - y_1) = 4a(x_2 - x_1) \Rightarrow \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1) = \frac{4a}{y_2 + y_1}$
Putting this in (1) gives us $y - y_1 = \frac{4a}{x_2 + x_1}(x - x_1)$
Now, when $Q \rightarrow P, x_2 \rightarrow x_1$ and $y_2 \rightarrow y_1$ so the above equation becomes

d:para.m: $y - y_1 = \frac{4a}{2y_1}(x - x_1) \Rightarrow y y_1 = 2a x + y_1^2 - 2a x_1$

d:sect2.d:para: Substituting $y_1^2 = 4a x_1$ we have \[ y y_1 = 2a(x + x_1) \tag{6.3}\]
which is the equation of the required tangent.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Normal at a Given Point on a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: We have obtained the equation of the tangent to a parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at $(x_1, y_1)$ as $yy_1 = 2a(x + x_1) \ldots$ (1), The slope of tangent is $\frac{2a}{y1}$.
The normal will be perpendicular to the tangent, and hence, its slope will be $-\frac{y_1}{2a}$.
Thus equation of normal would be \[y - y_1 = -\frac{y_1}{2a}(x - x_1) \tag{6.4}\]

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Normal in terms of its Slope
d:sect2.d:para: The normal to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at $(x_1, y_1)$ is $y - y_1 = -\frac{y_1}{2a}(x - x_1)$.
Let $-\frac{y_1}{2a} = m \Rightarrow y_1 = 2am$. Since $y_1^2 = 4a x_1 \Rightarrow 4a^2m^2 = 4ax_1 \Rightarrow x_1 = a m^2$
$\Rightarrow y - (-2a m) = m(x - a m^2) \Rightarrow y = mx - 2am - am^3$, which is the equation of the normal in terms of its slope.
Notes: The equation of the normal obtained is $y = mx - 2am - am^3$. This normal passes through $(x_1, y_1)$. Thus, $a m^3 + (2a - x_1) + m + y_1 = 0$.
This is a cubic equation in $m$, which will have three roots of which at least one will be real because complex roots occur in pair.
Any three points on the parabola, normals at which pass through a common point, are called co-normal points.

d:sect2.d:title: Parametric Equation of the Parabola $y^2 = 4a x$
d:sect2.d:para: The point $P$ whose coordinates are $x = at^2, y = 2at$ lies on the parabola $y^2 = 4a x$, which can be trivially verified by substituting in $y^2 = 4a x$.
This representation in which $x$ and $y$ are represented using a single parameter $t$ is called the parametric equation of the parabola.
The point $(at^2, 2at)$ is also referred to as the point '$t$'.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Chord of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Consider two points $(at_1^2, 2at_1)$ and $(at_2^2, 2at_2)$ on the parabola forming a chord.
The equation will be given by $y - 2at_1 = \frac{2at_2 - 2at_1}{at_2^2 - at_1^2}(x - at_1^2)$
is the equation of the the chord.

If this line passes through the focus i.e. $(a, 0)$ then $2a + 2at_1t_2 = 0 \Rightarrow t_1t_2 = -1$. Thus, if one point is $t$ then the condition for the chord to pass through the focus requires the other point to be $-\frac{1}{t}$.

d:sect2.d:title: Tangent and Normal at any Point $t$
d:sect2.d:para: The tangent to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at the point $(at^2, 2at)$ is given by
$y(2at) = 2a(x + a t^2) \Rightarrow ty = x + at^2$.
The normal to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at the point $(at^2, 2at)$ is given by
$y - 2at = -t(x - at^2) \Rightarrow y + t x = 2at + at^3$.

We see that two tangents at $t_1$ and $t_2$ have $(a t_1t_2, a(t_1 + t_2))$ as their point of intersection and the normals at the same points will have $\left(2a + a\left(t_1^2 + t_2^2 + t_1t_2\right), -a t_1t_2(t_1 + t_2)\right)$ as their point of intersection.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Chord of a Parabola whose middle point is $(x_1, y_1)$
d:sect2.d:para: Equation of the parabola is $y^2 = 4ax$. Let $AB$ be a chord of the parabola whose middle point is $P(x_1, y_1)$.
Equation of the chord is $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, where $m$ is the slope of $AB$.
Let $A = (x_2, y_2)$ and $B = (x_3, y_3) \Rightarrow y_2^2 = 4a x_2$ and $y_3^2 = 4a x_3$

d:para.m: $\therefore y_2^2- y_3^2 = 4a(x_2 - x_3) \Rightarrow \frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3} = \frac{4a}{y_2 + y_3}$

d:sect2.d:para: But $P$ is mid-point of $AB$, so we can write $y_2 + y_3 = 2y_1$
Thus, equation of the chord is $y - y_1 = \frac{2a}{y_1}(x - x_1) \Rightarrow y y_1 - 2a(x + x_1) = y_1^2 - 4a x_1$.

d:sect2.d:title: Tangents from a Point outside a Parabola to the Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4ax$ and $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a given point.
The equation of a tangent to the parabola is $y = m x + \frac{a}{m}$

$\Rightarrow m^2\alpha - \beta m + a = 0. D > 0 \Rightarrow \beta^2 - 4a\alpha > 0$ i.e. if the point lies outside the parabola then $m$ will be real and the equation will have two real roots, which gives us two tangents to the parabola from the point $P$.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of Pair of Tangents from a Point to a Parabola

d:figure.d:title: Pair of tangents from a point w.r.t. to a parabola

d:sect2.d:para: Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x$. Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be a point outside the parabola. Let a chord of the parabola through the point $P$ cut the parabola at $R$ and let $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ be any arbitrary point on the line $PR$. Let $R$ divide $PQ$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$, then
Since $R$ lies on the parabola, therefore $\left(\frac{\lambda\beta + y_1}{\lambda + 1}\right)^2 = 4a\frac{\lambda\alpha + x_1}{\lambda + 1}$
$\Rightarrow (\beta^2 - 4a\alpha)\lambda^2 + 2[\beta y_1 - 2a(\alpha + x_1)]\lambda + \left(y_1^2 - 4a x_1\right) = 0 \ldots$ (1)
Line $PQ$ will become a tangent to the parabola if the roots of the above equation (1) are equal
Hence, locus of $(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of pair of tangents from $P$ is $[y y_1 - 2a(x + x_1)]^2 = \left(y^2 - 4a x\right)\left(y_1^2 - 4a x_1\right)$
$\Rightarrow T^2 = SS_1$, where $T, S$ and $S_1$ have usual meanings.

d:sect2.d:para: Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x \ldots$ (1) Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a point outside the parabola. Let $PA$ and $PB$ be the two tangents from $P$ to the parabola (1). Let $PA$ and $PB$ be the two tangents from $P$ to the parabola (1).

d:sect2.d:para: Let $A = (x_1, y_1)$ and $B = (x_2, y_2)$. Equation of the tangent $PA$ is $yy_1 = 2a(x + x_1)$ and that of $PB$ is $y y_2 = 2a(x + x_2)$.
Since both the lines pass through $P$, therefore $\beta y_1 = 2a(\alpha + x_1)$ and $\beta y_2 = 2a(\alpha + x_2)$.
Now we consider the equation $y\beta = 2a(x + \alpha)$. We see that this line passes through both $A$ and $B$. Therefore, it is the equation of chord of contact $AB$ of point $P$ w.r.t. the parabola.

So the correct definition is here. Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be any point. The line whose equation is that of the tangent to $P$ to parabola whether $P$ lies on the curve or not is called the polar of point $P$ w.r.t. the parabola. According to this definition equation of polar of point $P(x_1, y_1)$ w.r.t. the parabola is $T = 0$ or $y y_1 = 2a(x + x_1)$.

d:sect2.d:title: Diameter of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Diameter of a conic is the locus of mid-points of a series of its parallel chords.
Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x\ldots$ (1)
Let $AB$ be one of the chords of a series of parallel chords having slope $m$. Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be the mid-point of chord $AB$, then equation of $AB$ will be $T = S_1$.
$\Rightarrow y\beta - 2a(x + \alpha) = \beta^2 - 4a\alpha \ldots$ (2)
Slope of this line is $frac{2a}{\beta}$. But slope of the line $AB$ is $m$, therefore $\frac{2a}{\beta} = m \Rightarrow beta = \frac{2a}{m}$.
Hence, locus of $P(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of diameter is \[ y = \frac{2a}{m} \tag{6.7}\]
Clearly, this line is parallel to the axis of the parabola.

d:sect2.d:title: The Optical Property of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: The tangent at any point $P$ on a parabola bisects the angle between the focal chord through $P$ and the perpendicular from $P$ on the directrix.
Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x \ldots$ (1)
Let $P(at^2, 2at)$ be a point on the parabola and let $PM \perp \text{ directrix}$.
Equation of the tangent to parabola at $P$ is $yt = x + at^2$. Slope of this tangent $PT$ is $\frac{1}{t} \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \frac{1}{t}$
Slope of $PS = \frac{2at}{a\left(t^2 - 1\right)} = \frac{\frac{2}{t}}{1 - \frac{1}{t^2}} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} = \tan2\theta$.
$\Rightarrow \angle PSX = 2\theta \Rightarrow \angle TPS = \angle PSX - \angle PTS = 2\theta - \theta = \theta$.
Hence, $\angle SPT = \angle MPT = \theta$.
Therefore $PT$ bisects $\angle MPS$.
The other property we know from physics is that rays coming from infinity are reflected by parabolas in such a manner that they pass through focus. We will prove that here.
Let $PN$ be normal to $PT$. In $\triangle PTN, \angle TPN = 90^\circ$ and $\angle PTN = \theta$
Since $PR \parallel TN, \therefore \angle RPN = \angle TNP = 90^\circ - \theta$
Also, $\angle SPN = 180^\circ - \angle PSN - \angle SNP = 180^\circ - 2\theta - \left(90^\circ - \theta\right) = 90^\circ - \theta$
$\therefore \angle SPN = \angle RPN$.
Thus, a ray parallel to the axis of parabola after reflection from parabola passes through the focus.

d:sect1.d:title: Ellipse
d:sect1.d:para: An ellipse is the locus of the point, which moves in the plane so that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point, and a fixed line is a constant, which is less than one.
The fixed point is called the focus, the constant ratio is called the eccentricity, and the fixed straight line is known as the directrix of the ellipse.
In the figure above, $S$ is the focus and $MM'$ the directrix. Let $P$ be any point on the ellipse, then $\frac{PS}{PN} = e < 1$.
Thus, we can find the equation of an ellipse when the coordinates of the focus, the equation of the directrix, and the eccentricity are known.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let $S$ be the focus and $M M'$ be the directrix of the ellipse. Draw $SH \perp MM'$, wed divide $SH$ internally and externally in the ratio $e: 1(e < 1)$ at points $A$ and $A'$ respectively, then
$\frac{AS}{AH} = e \ldots$ (1) and $\frac{A'S}{A'H} = e\ldots$ (2)
Clearly, $A$ and $A'$ will lie on the ellipse. Let $AA' = 2a$. Let $O$ be the mid-point of $AA'$. We take $O$ as the origin and $OA'$ and $OY$ as the $x$ and $y$ axes respectively.
From (1), $AS = e AH$ and from (2) $A'S = e A'H$.
$AS + A'S = e(AH + A'H) \Rightarrow 2a = (AH + AH + AA') = e(2Ah + 2a) \therefore A H = \frac{a}{e} - e$.
From (1) $AS = e AH = a - ae \therefore O S= OA - AS = ae \therefore S = (-ae, 0)$.
and $OH = OA + AH = \frac{a}{e}$.
Equation of $MM'$ is $x = -\frac{a}{e} \Rightarrow e x + a = 0$.
Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a point on ellipse. Draw $PN \perp MM'$
Now $\frac{PS}{PN} = e \Rightarrow PS^2 = e^2PN^2$
$\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{a^2\left(1 - e^2\right)} = 1$.
Let $b^2 = a^2\left(1 - e^2\right)$
Then the locus of $P$ is the equation of the ellipse, which is
It is clear that if $(ae, 0)$ is the focus, and $ex - a = 0$ is the directrix even then the ellipse will have the same equation.
Thus, the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ has two foci and two directrices.
A circle is a special limiting case of an ellipse whose major axis is $2a$, both foci approach the center and eccentricity approaches $0$.
A typical ellipse is given below:

As you can see an ellipse cuts $x$-axis at $(-a, 0)$ and $(a, 0)$, cuts $y$-axis at $(-b, 0)$ and $(b, 0)$. Equation of ellipse does not change when $x$ or $y$ are changed to $-x$ and $-y$, hence, an ellipse is symmetrical about $x$ and $y$ axes.
We have $y = \pm \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \Rightarrow a^2 - x^2 \geq 0 \Rightarrow -a \leq x \leq a$.
Similarly, $x = \pm \frac{a}{b} \sqrt{b^2 - y^2} \Rightarrow b^2 - x^2 \geq 0 \Rightarrow -b \leq y \leq b$.
We see that ellipse is bounded between $-a \leq x \leq a$ and $-b \leq y \leq b$ so an eclipse is a closed curve.
$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{b^2x}{b^2y}$. At $(-a, 0)$ and $(a, 0)$, the slope is not defined, and hence, tangent at $(-a, 0)$ and $(a, 0)$ will be perpendicular to $x$-axis.
At $(0, -b)$ and $(0, b), \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, therefore, at these points tangents are parallel to $x$-axis.

If $(x_1, y_1)$ lies on the curve, so does $(-x_1, -y_1)$. But $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(-x_1, -y_1)$ are points on the line through the origin and are equidistant from the origin. Hence, every chord through the origin $C$ is bisected at $C$. The point $C$ is, therefore, callled the center of the ellipse.

d:sect2.d:title: Second focus and second directrix of an ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let $P(x, y)$ be a point on the ellipse and let $C$ be its center. Let the equation of the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, where $b^2 = a^2\left(1 - e^2\right)\ldots$ (1)
Here $CA = CA' = a$ and $e$ is the eccentricity of the ellipse and the point $S$ and the line $QN$ are the focus and directrix respectively.
Let us take $S'$ and $Q'$ on the $x$-axis on that side of $C$ which is opposite to the side of $S$ such that $CS' = ae$ and $CQ' = \frac{a}{e}\ldots$ (2)
